course.title: Needs Analysis & Performance Program Design
course.owner: JR Romero, CSCS - Director of Training
course.evidence_pack: G3 102 Needs Analysis & Performance Program Design Evidence Pack
course.purpose: Teach a G3 Performance coach to make defensible programming decisions - not to write workouts.
course.prerequisite: G3 101 and active G3 Performance coaching status

nine_questions: What does this athlete's sport or role actually require?
What does this athlete currently possess?
Which differences do not matter enough to prioritize right now?
What is deliberately deprioritized, and at what accepted cost?
How do those decisions show up in the actual written program?
What evidence would make me change this program?

evidence_classes.name: Established Evidence
evidence_classes.teaching_rule: May be taught as established, bounded by population and context.

evidence_classes.name: Supported Practice
evidence_classes.teaching_rule: Taught as well-supported practice; the interpretive step must be stated.

evidence_classes.name: Emerging / Conditional Evidence
evidence_classes.teaching_rule: Taught as conditional; never the sole basis for a required behavior.

evidence_classes.name: Applied Coaching Inference
evidence_classes.teaching_rule: Taught explicitly as inference; must be labeled when taught.

evidence_classes.name: Historical / Practitioner Framework
evidence_classes.teaching_rule: Taught as framework and history; never as proof.

standing_labels.label: G3 Doctrine
standing_labels.note: Coaches teach and reason from it.

standing_labels.label: G3 Applied Standard
standing_labels.note: Organizational rule where evidence does not determine an answer.

standing_labels.label: Coach Judgment
standing_labels.note: No fixed answer; reasoning must be documented.

integrity_rules: No stage is skipped; a program without a documented priority stage is not a G3 program.
Changing a prescription requires revisiting the priority that produced it.
The model produces defensible decisions, not correct ones.
No automated scoring; any tool converting inputs into a recommended target requires Director of Training approval.

stages.name: DEMAND
stages.question: What does this sport, position, or role actually require?
stages.exit_criterion: Three to five demands named; peak separated from average
stages.common_failure: Listing every demand as important; using averages as the whole picture

stages.name: PROFILE
stages.question: What does this athlete currently possess?
stages.exit_criterion: Complete enough to program from; no item without a decision
stages.common_failure: Testing to fill a form; failing to record conditions

stages.name: GAP
stages.question: Which differences are real, and which are relevant?
stages.exit_criterion: Carried-forward and set-aside items both stated
stages.common_failure: Treating the lowest score as the biggest problem

stages.name: PRIORITY
stages.question: What earns the athlete's highest-quality effort right now?

stages.name: PRESCRIPTION
stages.question: What is the actual program, and does it reflect the priorities?
stages.exit_criterion: An outside coach can infer the priority from the order
stages.common_failure: Priority stated but contradicted by session order

stages.name: RESPONSE
stages.question: What is actually happening?
stages.exit_criterion: Working, not working, or cannot yet tell
stages.common_failure: Judging the program by competitive results

stages.name: ADJUST
stages.question: Change, hold, or progress - and why?
stages.exit_criterion: Every change has a reason that is not the calendar
stages.common_failure: Change for novelty; no record of reasoning

decision_model.gpi_rule: GPI output enters at PROFILE and is filtered at GAP. GPI never enters at PRIORITY.

doctrine.title: Needs analysis must change decisions
doctrine.statement: Assessment exists to improve coaching decisions. A test, metric, questionnaire, or observation earns its place when it can meaningfully influence exercise selection, training priority, load, volume, progression, regression, recovery, readiness modification, return-to-performance decisions, or program evaluation. G3 favors decision-useful information over maximal data collection.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Do not teach that a specific battery size is correct. Teach that unused data has a cost that must be earned.

doctrine.title: Sport demand is more than the average
doctrine.statement: Sport-demand analysis must consider movement, force, velocity, power, energetic, repeated-effort, and positional demands, competition and practice density, peak or worst-case passages, injury exposure, and season structure. Average match demands can conceal the highest-performance requirements.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Peak-demand evidence is largely locomotor and largely professional. Teach peak-demand thinking without claiming measurement precision the environment does not have.

doctrine.title: A deficit is not automatically a limiting factor
doctrine.statement: G3 distinguishes a measured deficit from a probable performance limiting factor. A deficit's claim strengthens when it matters to the sport or role, is meaningfully below the required level, can be changed, is relevant to current performance, can be addressed at acceptable cost, and deserves emphasis relative to competing priorities. Testing identifies information; coaching determines significance.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: No G3 material may state that a test identifies a limiting factor. The term 'confirmed limiting factor' is prohibited.

doctrine.title: Priority is a relevance x opportunity-cost decision
doctrine.statement: G3 does not adopt 'always train the greatest weakness.' Priority considers sport relevance, deficit magnitude, athlete level, training age, phase, injury/availability, adaptation potential, time, practice and competition demands, fatigue cost, interference, maintenance requirements, and expected performance return. A strength may deserve development; a weakness may deserve maintenance or no direct intervention.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Prioritization worksheets organize judgment; they never compute an answer. No weighted priority score may be created.

doctrine.title: Exercise selection serves adaptation
doctrine.statement: Do not confuse visual resemblance to sport with transfer. Selection considers desired adaptation, competency, loading potential, velocity, intent, range of motion, complexity, fatigue cost, risk/reward, equipment, history, training age, progression potential, and place in the total program.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting resemblance-as-transfer is not rejecting specificity of adaptation.

doctrine.title: Priority determines order
doctrine.statement: Exercises and qualities placed earlier in a session generally receive greater performance capacity. Session order reflects training priority rather than habit.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Order effects are clearest in untrained to moderately trained populations. Do not teach a numeric penalty for ordering second.

doctrine.title: Multiple qualities can be developed concurrently
doctrine.statement: Strength, speed, power, conditioning, and movement skill can coexist in a program. Concurrent does not mean equal emphasis: programs distinguish primary development, secondary development, maintenance, and exposure qualities. Interference is conditional and managed through sequencing, spacing, modality, volume, intensity, recovery, training status, and schedule.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: No numeric interference thresholds or mandatory spacing presented as evidence. G3 spacing conventions are Applied Standards.

doctrine.title: Individualization does not require unique programs for everyone
doctrine.statement: Standardize where athletes are similar; individualize where differences matter. Teams standardize session structure, movement categories, objectives, coaching language, and progression framework, and individualize through variation, load, volume, complexity, range of motion, progression rate, regression, substitution, and readiness adjustment.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Taught explicitly as applied inference, while binding as a G3 Applied Standard for team environments.

doctrine.title: Youth training is readiness-based, not age-myth-based
doctrine.statement: Supervised progressive resistance training is appropriate for youth. Readiness considers instructional responsiveness, psychological readiness, movement competency, maturity, training history, supervision, and progression.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The safety and efficacy claim is conditioned on supervision and progression; state both conditions whenever the claim is made.

doctrine.title: Autoregulation is a tool, not a religion
doctrine.statement: G3 may use RPE, RIR, velocity, performance feedback, structured readiness indicators, and coach observation. Autoregulation can improve individualization but is not universally superior to well-designed standardized programming.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Never teach that autoregulation beats a fixed program. Compare design quality against design quality.

doctrine.title: No single readiness metric runs the program
doctrine.statement: No single wellness score, jump score, HRV value, questionnaire, subjective rating, or wearable metric automatically dictates training. Readiness is interpreted through Baseline + Reliability + Context + Multiple Signals + Coaching Judgment.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Confident dashboards, composite scores, and automated recommendations require independent validation - including G3's own GPI outputs.

doctrine.title: Programs change for reasons
doctrine.statement: Programs do not need to change because four weeks passed, the athlete is bored, or novelty appears advanced. Change is justified by adaptation, stagnation, technical mastery, pain, athlete response, schedule, phase objectives, progression needs, changing sport demands, or poor fit.
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Absence of evidence for mandatory change is not evidence that programs should rarely change. A coach who never changes anything also fails this doctrine.

applied_standards.text: Every assessment item is traceable to at least one of the ten decision categories, documented when the battery is built.
The G3 decision model is the required reasoning sequence for all G3 program documentation.
Every team and sport-group program is preceded by a written Sport Demand Profile, reviewed annually or on change of level or role.
Demand profiles label every element measured, estimated, or assumed.
All six profile domains are completed for athletes carrying individual programs; team athletes carry domains (i)-(iv) at minimum.
Test conditions are recorded at the time of testing. A retest without recorded original conditions is reported as a new baseline, not as a change.
G3 written programming carries a Gap Statement with all three lists.
The phrase 'confirmed limiting factor' is prohibited in G3 documentation, education, and athlete communication.
Every program assigns an emphasis tier to every trained quality.
Every program carries a written opportunity-cost statement.
No G3 tool may compute a priority. Prioritization worksheets organize judgment; they do not output decisions.
Every exercise carries a stated intended adaptation and an emphasis tier in the program document.
G3 programs are built on standardized movement categories; individualization occurs within the category.
Sessions follow the standardized architecture, with the primary development quality positioned first after preparation unless a documented reason exists.
Every team session carries a written protection order for lost time.
Weekly plans display the emphasis tier against every quality trained.
Weekly plans are written against actual available training slots, with the primary quality assigned to the most reliable slots.

G3 spacing and sequencing conventions are organizational conventions, documented locally with a review date and taught with that label attached. G3 publishes no spacing threshold as an evidence-derived rule.
Every phase document states an objective, a progression plan for the primary quality, maintenance prescriptions with verification tests, and defined review points.
No G3 material publishes universal maintenance doses or mandatory phase lengths.
Every team template names its open individualization channels and who may adjust each.
Every movement category in a template carries a defined regression and progression.
Substitutions preserve intended adaptation, movement category, and emphasis tier.
Autoregulation operates within written decision boundaries; changes beyond them are logged decisions.
Formal autoregulation systems are not used as primary prescription tools in G3 Youth S&C.
No G3 readiness display may present an automated training recommendation.
Every program carries an adjustment log; holds are recorded as decisions.
Program evaluation reads process, then training, then performance, then outcome.
'We cannot yet tell' is an acceptable and expected review outcome.
Entry to loaded progressions is governed by readiness criteria, never by chronological age alone. Supervision ratio is part of the safety claim and is documented for every youth group.

G3 applies foundational resistance-training and program-design principles across sexes and does not publish sex-specific programming modifications where direct evidence is insufficient. Individual modification proceeds on individual grounds. Under review.
Athletes returning from injury re-enter the decision model at Stage 1. Medical clearance is a precondition, not a programming decision.

prohibited_claims.claim: Always train the weakest quality first.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported as a universal rule; relevance and opportunity cost vary.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Priority is a relevance x opportunity-cost decision (D4).

prohibited_claims.claim: Every athlete requires a completely unique program.
prohibited_claims.reason: Overstated; scalable templates can be defensible.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Standardize where similar, individualize where differences matter (D8).

prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; quality depends on how the template handles priorities, progressions, and modifications.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Evaluate the template, not the format.

prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; frequent rotation may obstruct evaluation of adaptation.

prohibited_claims.claim: Programs must change every four weeks.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: A phase is defined by objective, not duration (M9).

prohibited_claims.claim: One periodization model is universally best.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported and conditional; effectiveness depends on context and implementation.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Model literacy and defended choice; models taught as Class E.

prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; some deficits are neither priorities nor causal drivers.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Deficit is not a limiting factor (D3).

prohibited_claims.claim: More exercises make a program more complete.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; added content dilutes focus and adds cost.
Unsupported; visual specificity is not proof of transfer.

prohibited_claims.claim: Fatigue proves that training is effective.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; fatigue may reflect overload, poor timing, or insufficient recovery.

prohibited_claims.claim: Every physical quality must improve simultaneously.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; prioritization and maintenance are necessary.

prohibited_claims.claim: One readiness metric can determine daily training.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; no single metric is an established trigger.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Baseline + Reliability + Context + Multiple Signals + Judgment (D11).

prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; well-designed versions often produce similar outcomes.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Autoregulation is a tool, not an upgrade (D10).

prohibited_claims.claim: Exact universal maintenance doses exist for every quality.
prohibited_claims.reason: Unsupported; doses vary too much for precise universal rules.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Maintenance as defended reduction with verification test (M9).

prohibited_claims.claim: Resistance training is unsafe for youth or must wait for a given age.
prohibited_claims.reason: Contradicted by strong evidence, conditioned on supervision and progression.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Readiness-based youth training (D9). Do not overstate in either direction.

prohibited_claims.claim: A test identified this athlete's limiting factor.
prohibited_claims.reason: Field tests identify deficits and associations, not causes.
prohibited_claims.taught_instead: Probable limiting factor as coaching judgment (D3).

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Indirect; field tests show deficits and associations, not causes. Identified research gap.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: Which probable limiting factors to carry, and how confidently.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Literature is stronger on the need to prioritize than on how.
Maintenance likely requires less dose than development; exact doses underdetermined.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: The dose for this athlete, schedule, and quality.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: No direct evidence supports frequent rotation; restrained variation aids evaluation.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: When an exercise has done its work.

judgment_areas.g3_standard: Model literacy taught; no model adopted as doctrine.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: Which model's logic fits this athlete and season.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Practice-based and inferential; acknowledged research gap.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: How many channels to open at a given ratio.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: No single metric established as a trigger.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: What convergence justifies a change today.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Source set does not support strong sex-specific program-design claims.
Adult evidence extrapolated; limited direct youth evidence.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: How much perceptual input to use with a given adolescent.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Peak-demand evidence largely locomotor and professional; translation is interpretive.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: Which peak demands actually shape this program.

judgment_areas.evidence_position: Conditional; mechanisms and practical thresholds unsettled.
judgment_areas.coach_judgment: Sequencing for this week and this schedule.

competencies.title: Conduct a basic sport needs analysis
competencies.observable_standard: Produces a written demand profile across all twelve categories, with elements labeled measured/estimated/assumed, for a sport and role they coach.

competencies.title: Identify relevant sport demands
competencies.observable_standard: Ranks the three to five demands that will shape the program and distinguishes average from peak-passage demands.

competencies.title: Construct an athlete profile
competencies.observable_standard: Produces a profile across all six domains with recorded testing conditions and no item unconnected to a decision.

competencies.title: Interpret testing within measurement limitations
competencies.observable_standard: States whether a change exceeds typical error and whether it is practically significant; declines to act inside the noise band.

competencies.title: Distinguish deficit from probable limiting factor
competencies.observable_standard: Produces a gap statement with all three lists and uses no causal language.

competencies.title: Establish defensible priorities
competencies.observable_standard: Assigns emphasis tiers to every quality and writes a complete opportunity-cost statement.

competencies.title: Select exercises based on adaptation
competencies.observable_standard: States intended adaptation for every exercise and rejects at least one candidate in writing.

competencies.title: Order exercises based on priority
competencies.observable_standard: Builds a session whose order an outside coach reads back as the stated priority; provides a protection order.

competencies.title: Organize concurrent qualities
competencies.observable_standard: Builds a deliverable week with visible tiers and annotated sequencing, labeling convention versus evidence.

competencies.title: Distinguish development from maintenance
competencies.observable_standard: Prescribes maintenance as a defended reduction with a scheduled verification test.

competencies.title: Individualize within a group structure
competencies.observable_standard: Builds a template with named channels, authority levels, and pathways, deliverable at the stated ratio.

competencies.title: Use basic autoregulation appropriately
competencies.observable_standard: Applies RPE/RIR/velocity within written boundaries appropriate to population; escalates as a logged decision.

competencies.title: Interpret readiness cautiously
competencies.observable_standard: Applies the five-component formula; makes no single-metric decision; identifies required convergence.

competencies.title: Monitor program response
competencies.observable_standard: Completes a four-layer review in order and interprets retests against error.

competencies.title: Justify program modifications
competencies.observable_standard: Maintains an adjustment log with trigger, reasoning, expected effect, and review date; logs holds.

competencies.title: Programming defense (terminal)
competencies.observable_standard: Walks a real program end to end through the decision model, out loud, under questioning, answering all nine questions.

modules.title: What Needs Analysis Is For
modules.framing_statement: Needs analysis is not a form. It is the reason your program looks the way it does.

lessons.title: The purpose problem: descriptive vs decisional assessment
Why the evidence supports this indirectly

objectives: M1.1 State the purpose of needs analysis in decision terms
M1.2 Apply the decision test to any proposed assessment item
M1.3 Name the ten decision categories
M1.4 Describe the costs of undecidable data
M1.5 Reproduce the decision model from memory
M1.6 State the evidence standing of the model
common_errors: Presenting a needs analysis as a diagnosis
Treating the model as a form completed after the program

modules.title: Analyzing Sport Demands
modules.framing_statement: The average tells you what the sport usually asks. The peak tells you what it asks when it matters.
objectives: M2.1 Build a demand profile across twelve categories
M2.2 Distinguish average from peak demands
M2.3 Explain rolling averages vs fixed epochs
M2.4 Analyze positional differences
M2.5 Account for density and season structure
M2.6 Produce a defensible profile without tracking technology
common_errors: Treating one position's profile as the sport's
Adopting professional profiles for scholastic rosters

modules.title: Building the Athlete Profile
modules.framing_statement: The profile is not everything you know about the athlete. It is everything you will actually use.

lessons.title: Training age is not chronological age
Movement competency at the depth the decision needs
Reliability, typical error, practical significance introduced

objectives: M3.1 Construct a profile from six domains
M3.2 Apply the decision test to every item
M3.3 Record measurement conditions
M3.4 Assess movement competency appropriately
M3.5 Apply youth readiness criteria
M3.6 Integrate GPI at the correct stage
M3.7 State reliability limitations
common_errors: Profile built from test numbers only
Extensive youth testing to appear rigorous

modules.title: From Test Result to Limiting Factor
modules.framing_statement: The test tells you what the number is. It never tells you what to do.

lessons.title: Two different objects: deficit vs limiting factor

objectives: M4.1 Define and use both terms correctly
M4.2 Apply the reality filter
M4.3 Apply the relevance filter
M4.4 State the six conditions
M4.5 Explain why field testing shows association not cause
M4.6 Produce a three-list gap statement
M4.7 Explain limits of normative comparison
common_errors: Reading the lowest bar as the target
A gap statement with only one list

modules.title: Establishing Training Priorities
modules.framing_statement: Priority is a decision about where the athlete's best effort goes, and what you give up to put it there.

lessons.title: Why 'train the weakness' is not a rule
When a weakness is tiered down

objectives: M5.1 Reject the universal weakness-first rule with reasoning
M5.2 Assign emphasis tiers
M5.3 Write an opportunity-cost statement
M5.4 Weigh considerations without scoring them
M5.5 Defend developing a strength
M5.6 Defend tiering down a weakness
M5.7 Distinguish evidence, standard, and judgment

modules.title: Exercise Selection
modules.framing_statement: Every exercise is an answer to a question. If you cannot state the question, remove the exercise.
objectives: M6.1 Select from intended adaptation
M6.2 Apply the fourteen considerations
M6.3 Explain why visual specificity is not transfer
M6.4 Match complexity to competency
M6.5 Evaluate loading, velocity, ROM, fatigue cost
M6.6 Justify exercise count by focus
M6.7 Build a movement-category framework
common_errors: Choosing because it looks like the sport

modules.title: Building the Training Session
modules.framing_statement: Whatever you put first is what you decided mattered most, whether or not you meant to decide it.

lessons.title: Session quality as coaching, not layout

objectives: M7.1 Order a session by priority
M7.2 Explain order evidence and its boundaries
M7.3 Build G3 session architecture
M7.4 Position qualities by tier
M7.5 Detect priority-order mismatch
M7.6 Protect priority when time is lost
common_errors: Conditioning early in a strength session
Ordering by habit or equipment flow
Front-loading so nothing after is executed
Letting the schedule decide what is cut

modules.title: Building the Training Week
modules.framing_statement: The week is where programming stops being a list and starts being a system.
objectives: M8.1 Organize concurrent development
M8.2 Explain conditional interference

modules.title: Building the Training Phase

modules.title: Individualization at Scale
modules.framing_statement: Forty athletes, one coach, one hour. Individualization that cannot survive that room is a theory.
objectives: M10.1 Explain why unique programs are not required
M10.2 Identify what to standardize and individualize

modules.title: Autoregulation & Readiness

objectives: M11.1 Define autoregulation and its legitimate inputs

modules.title: Monitoring & Program Adjustment

M12.2 Explain why outcomes cannot evaluate training quality
M12.3 Interpret retests against error

M12.6 Maintain an adjustment log
M12.7 Reject fatigue as evidence
M12.8 Defend a decision under questioning

cases.title: Middle-School Athlete
cases.situation_summary: 12-year-old, no training history, high instructional responsiveness, 18-athlete group with one coach, two 50-minute sessions weekly. Parent asks for high-school-style testing and raises a lifting-safety concern.
cases.decision_prompt: What does the assessment consist of, what does the program prioritize, and what do you say to the parent?
failure_modes: Complexity beyond group competency and supervision ratio
Body composition with no attached decision

cases.title: High-School Team-Sport Athlete
cases.situation_summary: 16-year-old outside hitter, second year of structured training, tournament-format competition, eight-week pre-season, three G3 slots against four practices. Strength in bottom quartile; repeated-jump retention declining; jump output high.
cases.decision_prompt: What is prioritized in this block, what is deliberately not prioritized, and how is the week ordered?
failure_modes: Selecting the lowest GPI sub-score by default
Sex-specific loading rules asserted as evidence

cases.title: Collegiate Team
cases.situation_summary: 28 athletes, four position groups, mid-season, three-match week then a bye, five-week block with two doubleheaders and a road trip. Two slots weekly with one lost roughly every other week. Two coaches. Six low-training-age athletes; two returning from injury.
cases.decision_prompt: Build the match week and bye week; state tier movement, individualization delivery, and what cannot be achieved.
failure_modes: Bye week as catch-up for every quality

cases.title: Athlete With a Testing Deficit
cases.situation_summary: 17-year-old starter with the lowest lower-body strength score in the program across four occasions (well outside typical error), the highest approach jump and repeated-jump retention on the team, full availability, no pain, sound landing mechanics. GPI renders the score red; sport coach and parent have seen it.
cases.decision_prompt: Does this deficit become the primary programming target, and what do you say to the sport coach and parent?
failure_modes: Lowest score as target by default
Promising to fix the number for the report
Resolving it as measurement error when the data rules that out
GPI entering the model at Stage 4

cases.title: Poor Readiness Day
cases.situation_summary: In-season Tuesday, squad's protected strength session. One athlete's wellness composite is two points low (sleep, soreness); platform shows amber and suggests reduction. Warm-up normal, bar speed normal, RPE as expected, jump within typical error, exam the night before, no pain. Sport coach has seen the amber display.
cases.decision_prompt: What happens with the session, and what is the reasoning?
failure_modes: Treating a pain report as subject to the convergence rule

automatic_zero_conditions: prohibited claim presented as rule or evidence
session order contradicting stated priority without documented reason
causal language applied to a field test
published universal maintenance dose or mandatory phase length

defense_rubric.pass: 11/15, no dimension below 2, never 0 on evidence honesty

pass_standards.applied: at standard or better, one revision permitted

item_writing_rules: No item answerable from a single memorized sentence outside the knowledge band.
Every scenario item commits the learner before feedback.
Distractors are real coaching errors drawn from the prohibited claims and module error lists.
No key may depend on a claim classified C, D, or E.
No key may depend on an unmapped citation tag.
Where multiple answers are defensible, the item is a decision item scored on reasoning.
Every item carries module, competency, doctrine, evidence class, level, and key source metadata.

sign_offs.title: Assessment & Profile Sign-Off
observed_behaviors: Administers a movement competency screen competently and safely
Explains testing purpose in plain, non-alarming language
Records testing conditions without prompting
States which decision each battery item informs
Uses 'measured deficit' and 'probable limiting factor' correctly
Declines to interpret change inside typical error
States youth safety claims with supervision and progression conditions
assessor_questions: Why is this item in your battery?
What would you have done differently if this result were the opposite?
Which differences did you set aside, and why?
What are the conditions of this test, and why did you record them?

sign_offs.title: Program Build & Session Delivery Sign-Off
observed_behaviors: Delivers a session as written with the primary block protected
Coaches the primary quality actively rather than supervising
Teaches a selected exercise to the standard its adaptation requires
Applies the protection order when time is lost

citation_integrity_flags.handling: Claims referencing unmapped tags are carried at reduced confidence and always rest on mapped support. No assessment key may depend on them. Resolve or rewrite before external publication.

production_note.statement: Unresolved citation tags do not block internal G3 or NovaKore production. No assessment key may depend solely on an unresolved citation. Before external publication, third-party CEU recognition, accreditation submission, or public release, every unresolved tag must be mapped to a verified itemized source or its dependent language rewritten onto mapped support. Missing sources are never to be invented or inferred.

manual_verification_required: change-threshold conventions for G3 testing contexts
precise maintenance doses by quality and phase
skepticism_flags: vendor monitoring claims are not evidence
practitioner summaries inform terminology, not causation
confident readiness dashboards require independent validation, including G3's own GPI

data_layer_constraints: A session cannot publish unless every exercise carries intended_adaptation and emphasis_tier. (AS-12)
A phase cannot publish if any maintenance-tier quality lacks a scheduled verification test. (AS-19, AS-20)
A priority_sheet cannot publish without a complete opportunity_cost_statement. (AS-10)
A test_record without recorded conditions is flagged and treated as a new baseline. (AS-06)
No entity may expose a computed priority, composite readiness recommendation, or automated training instruction. (AS-11, AS-26)
gap_statement requires all three arrays present; empty arrays must be explicitly confirmed.
Free text containing 'confirmed limiting factor' is rejected at save. (AS-08)
